So java_type survives deepcopy. But wait — there's a subtlety: `JavaObject.__init__` requires (java_type, fields); deepcopy doesn't call `__init__` (uses `__new__` + state), so java_type restored from `__dict__`. OK.

But crucial bug candidate: `JavaObject` inherits dict; code does `{'__type__': ..., **obj}` etc. And in engine at line 911: `obj = JavaObject(self.p.nodes[tid]['fqn'],{'__type__':...})`. At line 933: `JavaObject(self.p.nodes[tid]['fqn'], {'__type__': receiver_type, ...})` — note it uses `receiver_type` as `__type__` but `self.p.nodes[tid]['fqn']` as java_type. That's fine.

(a) `standard_type` (line 823-834): `if self.p.resolve_type(name,meta['module'],meta['file']): return False` — resolves any name to a type in project. Then `if name==fqn:return True` — calling `standard_type('java.lang.Integer','java.lang.Integer')` returns True when name is fully qualified and not resolving to a project type. If a project defines its own `java.lang.Integer` class? Unlikely; resolve_type of "java.lang.Integer" would probably not match project types. Fine.

`if name!=fqn.rsplit('.',1)[-1]:return False` — so name must be simple `Integer`. Then examine imports of the file. If explicit import of `Integer` from another package exists → return explicit==[fqn], i.e., False if `import other.library.Integer;`. Test 5 covers that. If no explicit import of that simple name, returns True if fqn starts with java.lang. or wildcard import of the package. That means: a file that has a project class named `Integer` in the same package (e.g., `com.x.Integer`) — would `resolve_type('Integer', module, file)` resolve it to the project class?
